advances: Establishes absolute-coefficient actual second and third depth moments for arbitrary heterogeneous products of complete globally affine lattice factors with parity occupancy at most two and at most four distinct weights. The new common mixed-pair estimate gives a stronger occupied-capacity conclusion for midpoint-closed exact-product tables with arbitrarily many homogeneous weight levels, arbitrarily many midpoint centers, and unbounded common score. A single selection across the entire product pays the coefficient once. The four-height class is included without an atomic-activity assumption or a same-weight energy baseline.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. All cited predecessors are the five declared accepted facts; their uses and capacity or notation maps are specified above.
proof:
Fix first one factor satisfying (2). Every row contains its center and is closed under reflection about that center. For every \(x\in R_j\), the midpoint equality, including the trivial central case, gives
\(p_xp_{2j-x}=p_j^2\). Therefore every geometric row summand equals \(p_j\), and \(\kappa_j\) is uniform on its full row. If \(w_x=w_j\), the same equality gives \(w_{2j-x}=w_j\). Conversely, equal endpoint weights imply that both equal the positive midpoint weight. Thus \(\widehat R_j\) consists exactly of the equal-weight reflection orbits, is symmetric, and contains \(j\) once. Its score is zero throughout, and \(\widehat H_p(j)=p_j|\widehat R_j|\ge p_j\).

Since \(|A|\le2K\), the power-mean inequality gives
$$
E\ge K^2\sum_{j\in A}p_j^3
\ge\frac{K^2}{|A|^2}\ge\frac14.
\tag{10}
$$
Let \(\mu_\eta\) denote the original mass of occupied parity class \(\eta\), and put
\(\chi(p)=\sum_jp_jH_p(j)\). The correspondence
\((j,x)\longleftrightarrow(x,2j-x)\) bijects full oriented row entries with ordered same-parity pairs. Its inverse midpoint belongs to \(A\) by (2), and the equality of midpoint products makes each contribution \(p_j\sqrt{p_xp_{2j-x}}\) equal to the endpoint product. Consequently
$$
\chi(p)=\sum_\eta\mu_\eta^2\ge\frac1K,
\qquad b(p)\ge\chi(p)^2,
\qquad F\ge1.
\tag{11}
$$
Every diagonal pair is counted once in this identity. If there are no unequal-weight same-parity pairs, every full row is its same-weight row. In that case \(E=F\ge1\) and every score vanishes.

Now impose the common mixed-pair hypothesis and suppose \(E<1\). Let \(J\) be the number of unordered unequal-weight same-parity pairs. The preceding paragraph shows \(J>0\). Fix their common raw weights \(u<v\), and define \(T,\rho\) by (7). Each mixed midpoint has raw weight \(\sqrt{uv}\); its two oriented scores are \(T\) and \(-T\). Every other reflection orbit has zero score. The original normalizer in these statements is still \(Z\).

Use the unnormalized occupied parity defect
$$
\mathcal D_{\mathrm{un}}=\sum_{\eta\text{ occupied}}(K\mu_\eta-1)^2
=K^2\sum_\eta\mu_\eta^2-K.
\tag{12}
$$
Thus \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{un}}/K\), not \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{un}}\), is the normalized defect \(\mathcal D\) of 31c9b0b9219d18d9. Removing exactly the two orientations of every mixed pair from the identity (11) gives
$$
\widehat\chi(p)=\sum_\eta\mu_\eta^2-\frac{2J\rho^2}{K^2},
\qquad
K\widehat\chi(p)=1+\frac{\mathcal D_{\mathrm{un}}-2J\rho^2}{K},
\qquad E\ge(K\widehat\chi(p))^2.
\tag{13}
$$
The last inequality is Cauchy--Schwarz under the full original center law. Since \(0<K\widehat\chi(p)<1\), it follows that
\(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{un}}<2J\rho^2\).

Each mixed pair occupies its own parity class: occupancy at most two makes that class consist precisely of its endpoints. In particular \(J\le K\). All these \(J\) classes have the same scaled mass
\(K(u+v)/Z=2\rho\cosh T\). Their contributions to (12) imply
$$
J(2\rho\cosh T-1)^2
\le\mathcal D_{\mathrm{un}}<2J\rho^2,
\qquad
\rho(2\cosh T-\sqrt2)<1.
\tag{14}
$$
The latter inequality follows from \(2\rho\cosh T-1<\sqrt2\rho\); its coefficient of \(\rho\) is positive. If \(T\ge T_0\), then
\(2\cosh T-\sqrt2=e^T+e^{-T}-\sqrt2\ge e^T/2\), since \(e^T\ge4096\) and \(\sqrt2<2\). Hence
\(\rho<2e^{-T}\le1/2048<1/64\), proving the first assertion of (8).

For the rest of the scalar argument assume \(T\ge T_0\). Write
\(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{mid}}=\lbrace j\in A:w_j=\sqrt{uv}\rbrace\),
\(N_{\mathrm{mid}}=|\mathcal A_{\mathrm{mid}}|\), and let \(C_{\mathrm{mid}}\) be the number of parity classes occupied by this set. These count all atoms of that weight, including those that are not mixed midpoints. They are nonempty because \(J>0\). Every such class is pure: if an atom of weight \(\sqrt{uv}\) had a different-weight companion in its parity class, that pair would have to have endpoint-weight multiset \(\lbrace u,v\rbrace\), whereas \(u<\sqrt{uv}<v\). This is impossible. Each of the \(C_{\mathrm{mid}}\) classes therefore has one or two atoms, all of scaled probability \(\rho\). It follows that
$$
N_{\mathrm{mid}}\le2C_{\mathrm{mid}},\qquad
C_{\mathrm{mid}}(1-2\rho)^2
\le\mathcal D_{\mathrm{un}}<2J\rho^2.
\tag{15}
$$
The squared bound uses \(0<\rho<1/2\). It applies to each entire pure class and does not assign separate capacities to different midpoint rows.

For \(j\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{mid}}\), let \(h_{\mathrm{equal},j}=|\widehat R_j|\), and let \(r_j\) be the number of unordered mixed pairs with midpoint \(j\). Then \(\sum_jr_j=J\) and \(|R_j|=h_{\mathrm{equal},j}+2r_j\). Outside \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{mid}}\), the full and same-weight rows coincide. Using the exact geometric row summands and then Cauchy--Schwarz on all the \(r_j\) gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
G
&=\frac{\rho^3}{K}\sum_{j\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{mid}}}
  \bigl((h_{\mathrm{equal},j}+2r_j)^2-h_{\mathrm{equal},j}^2\bigr)\\
&\ge\frac{4\rho^3}{K}\sum_jr_j^2
\ge\frac{4\rho^3J^2}{KN_{\mathrm{mid}}}
\ge\frac{2\rho^3J^2}{KC_{\mathrm{mid}}}
>\frac{\rho J(1-2\rho)^2}{K}>0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{16}
$$
The last strict inequality uses (15). No restriction on any individual \(r_j\) or on the number of centers has entered this estimate.

Put \(a_{\mathrm{eq}}=K\widehat\chi(p)\) only in the following deficit calculation. By (13), \(0<a_{\mathrm{eq}}<1\), so
$$
\begin{aligned}
1-E&\le1-a_{\mathrm{eq}}^2
\le2(1-a_{\mathrm{eq}})
=\frac{2(2J\rho^2-\mathcal D_{\mathrm{un}})}K
\le\frac{4J\rho^2}K,\\
d=-\log E&\le\frac{1-E}{E}
\le\frac{16J\rho^2}K\le16\rho^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{17}
$$
Here (10) gives \(E\ge1/4\), and the final inequality uses \(J\le K\). Combining (16)-(17), and using \((1-2\rho)^2\ge49/64\), yields
$$
d\le21\rho G,
\tag{18}
$$
because \(16\cdot64/49=1024/49<21\).

If \(0<G\le1\), then \(1-E\le d\le21\rho G<G/2\), because \(\rho<1/64\). Therefore \(F=E+G\ge1+G/2>1\) and
\(g=\log F\ge\log(1+G/2)\ge G/4\). The last inequality follows by integrating \(1/(1+s)\ge1/2\) for \(0\le s\le G/2\). Thus \(d\le84\rho g\). If \(G\ge1\), then \(F\ge5/4\), so \(g\ge\log(5/4)\ge1/5\), using \(\log x\ge(x-1)/x\) for \(x\ge1\). Equation (17) gives
\(d\le16\rho^2\le\rho/4\le(5/4)\rho g\le84\rho g\).
Both cases prove \(g>0\) and
\(d\le84\rho g\le168e^{-T}g\).

Uniformity of the full geometric row law gives
\(V_j=2r_jT^2/(h_{\mathrm{equal},j}+2r_j)\) on \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{mid}}\), and \(V_j=0\) elsewhere. Consequently the exact full-row score numerator is
$$
F\nu=\frac{\rho^3}{K}\sum_{j\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{mid}}}
2r_j(h_{\mathrm{equal},j}+2r_j)T^2
\le T^2G.
\tag{19}
$$
Indeed \(2r(h+2r)\le4r(h+r)=(h+2r)^2-h^2\) for \(r\ge0\), \(h\ge1\), term by term. Since \(F/E>1\),
\(G/F=1-E/F\le\log(F/E)=g+d\). Thus
$$
\nu\le T^2(g+d)\le(1+84\rho)T^2g\le3T^2g.
\tag{20}
$$
Equations (18)-(20) prove all of (8) with \(C=256\). In particular, the zero-score choice is the whole same-weight background, including every central atom; it need not have atomic energy at least one.

We next identify the other factors that can be combined with these labels. For any factor satisfying (2), occupancy at most two, and \(|Y_j(x)|\le T_0\) on every full row, accepted fact 31c9b0b9219d18d9 applies with \(M=2\), its score bound \(T=T_0\), and exactly its occupied count \(K\). Its \(H_p,b,\kappa,Y,V,q,\nu\) are precisely those in (6), with the same \(p,w,Z\). It supplies
$$
K^2b(p)\ge1,\qquad \nu\le C_0\log(K^2b(p)).
\tag{21}
$$
There is no midpoint-degree restriction in that fact. A common-pair factor with \(E<1\) and \(T<T_0\) satisfies this score hypothesis, since every nonzero score is \(T\).

For a complete globally affine factor whose distinct log weights are separated by at least \(\log64\), accepted fact 4e2de5c00a49d7b9 gives
$$
2^{2n}b_{\mathrm{equal}}\ge1
\quad\text{and same-weight selected price zero}.
\tag{22}
$$
Its original law and normalizer, and its hats, agree with ours. Its capacity in (22) is specifically \(2^n\). This application does not replace it by the occupied count \(K\).

Every factor in the four-weight assertion belongs to one of the preceding groups. Convex completeness gives its midpoint closure, and its global affine log weight gives the exact product in (2). Let \(\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_m\) be its distinct log weights, where \(m\le4\). Any unequal-weight same-parity pair forces a nontrivial arithmetic triple among these values, with its midpoint value between its endpoint values. If there is at most one such arithmetic triple in the whole spectrum, every unequal-weight pair therefore has the same two raw endpoint weights. If there is no such pair, it is already an allowed common-pair factor. This proves the common-pair alternative for every spectrum with at most one arithmetic triple.

If there are at least two arithmetic triples, necessarily \(m=4\). Write the positive adjacent gaps as
\(\Delta_1=\lambda_2-\lambda_1\), \(\Delta_2=\lambda_3-\lambda_2\), and \(\Delta_3=\lambda_4-\lambda_3\). The four possible triples, in the order \((1,2,3),(1,2,4),(1,3,4),(2,3,4)\), impose respectively
$$
\Delta_1=\Delta_2,\qquad
\Delta_1=\Delta_2+\Delta_3,\qquad
\Delta_1+\Delta_2=\Delta_3,\qquad
\Delta_2=\Delta_3.
\tag{23}
$$
The first and second equalities force \(\Delta_3=0\); the second and third force \(\Delta_2=0\); and the third and fourth force \(\Delta_1=0\). These three pairs are impossible. The remaining pairs, first with third, first with fourth, and second with fourth, give respectively
\((\Delta_1,\Delta_2,\Delta_3)=(\delta,\delta,2\delta),(\delta,\delta,\delta),(2\delta,\delta,\delta)\), with \(\delta>0\). This exhausts the six pairs of equalities, and hence every spectrum with at least two triples. Equivalently, the spectrum is a translate of a positive multiple of
$$
\lbrace0,1,2,4\rbrace,\qquad
\lbrace0,1,2,3\rbrace,\qquad
\lbrace0,2,3,4\rbrace.
\tag{24}
$$
In each case \(\delta\) is the minimum distinct log gap and \(\lambda_4-\lambda_1\le4\delta\). Thus every row score has magnitude at most \(2\delta\). If \(\delta\le\log64\), all scores are at most \(T_0\), so (21) applies. If \(\delta>\log64\), every distinct log gap is greater than \(\log64\), so (22) applies. This proves the required exhaustive classification, including the boundary \(\delta=\log64\) in the bounded-score group.

We now give one product argument that combines common-pair factors, the bounded-score factors of (21), and the zero-score factors of (22). For the first assertion of the theorem, every factor is assigned to the common-pair group. For the four-weight assertion, use the classification just proved. For a common-pair or bounded-score factor assign the capacity \(k_i=K_i\); for a factor assigned to (22) assign \(k_i=2^{n_i}\). The symbols \(k_i\) denote these proof capacities only, and never alter \(p_i\) or \(Z_i\). In particular \(k_i\le2^{n_i}\) always, and all capacities are exactly occupied counts in the first assertion.

For a common-pair factor with \(E_i\ge1\), choose its same-weight rows, which have scaled energy at least one and price zero. This includes every common-pair factor with no unequal-weight pairs. For a common-pair factor with \(E_i<1\) and \(T_i<T_0\), choose its full rows and regard it as a bounded-score factor in (21). All other common-pair factors have \(E_i<1\), \(T_i\ge T_0\), and carry the single label with \(d_i,g_i,T_i\) from (8). A retained label means all full rows of that factor; a discarded label means all its same-weight rows. All factors assigned to (21) use full rows, and all factors assigned to (22) use same-weight rows.

Perform one binning of all the remaining labels, as in the scalar binning proof of accepted fact f5955204a537cb64. Its label quantities \(\gamma,\delta,t\) correspond here to \(g_i,d_i,T_i\). We reproduce the argument using the new valid constant \(C=256\); none of that fact's one-center or two-center geometric hypotheses is invoked. For every integer \(m\ge0\), let
\(I_m=\lbrace i:T_i\in[m,m+1)\text{ for a remaining label}\rbrace\) and \(G_m=\sum_{i\in I_m}g_i\). Retain all labels in the bin if and only if \(G_m\ge4C(m+1)^2\). Only finitely many bins are nonempty. For a retained bin put \(W_m=C(m+1)^2G_m\). Equation (8) gives total price at most \(W_m\) in that bin, and the retention inequality gives \(G_m\ge2\sqrt{W_m}\). In a discarded bin the total logarithmic deficit is bounded by
$$
\sum_{i\in I_m}d_i\le Ce^{-m}G_m
<4C^2e^{-m}(m+1)^2.
\tag{25}
$$
An empty bin has deficit zero. Since
\(\sum_{m\ge0}(m+1)^2r^m=(1+r)/(1-r)^3\) for \(0\le r<1\), and \(e^{-1}<1/2\), the total discarded deficit is at most \(48C^2\).

Use stars for the rows chosen by this whole-product procedure, reserving hats for the same-weight selection in (6). For each factor define
$$
\begin{aligned}
H_i^*(j)&=\sum_{x\in R_{i,j}^*}\sqrt{p_{i,x}p_{i,2j-x}},&
b_i^*&=\sum_{j\in A_i}p_{i,j}H_i^*(j)^2,\\
\kappa_{i,j}^*(x)&=\frac{\sqrt{p_{i,x}p_{i,2j-x}}}{H_i^*(j)},&
q_{i,j}^*&=\frac{p_{i,j}H_i^*(j)^2}{b_i^*},\\
V_{i,j}^*&=\mathbb E_{\kappa_{i,j}^*}Y_{i,j}^2,&
\nu_i^*&=\sum_{j\in A_i}q_{i,j}^*V_{i,j}^*.
\end{aligned}
\tag{26}
$$
Here \(Y_{i,j}\) is exactly the full-row score in (6), restricted to the chosen row. The stars equal the full quantities when a full row is chosen; choosing all same-weight rows gives \(b_i^*=b_{\mathrm{equal},i}\) and \(\nu_i^*=0\). Every center remains in the sum for \(b_i^*\).

Let \(B_{\log}\) be the sum of \(\log(k_i^2b(p_i))\) over all factors using the bounded-score estimate (21), with empty sum zero. Then \(B_{\log}\ge0\), and their total price is at most \(C_0B_{\log}\). Summing all factor logarithmic energies and all selected prices gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
S_g:=\sum_i\log(k_i^2b_i^*)
&\ge B_{\log}+\sum_{m\text{ retained}}G_m-48C^2,\\
\sum_i\nu_i^*&\le C_0B_{\log}+\sum_{m\text{ retained}}W_m.
\end{aligned}
\tag{27}
$$
The other factors have nonnegative logarithmic energy and zero price. By subadditivity of the square root and \(G_m\ge2\sqrt{W_m}\),
$$
\begin{aligned}
S_g-2\sqrt{\sum_i\nu_i^*}
&\ge B_{\log}-2\sqrt{C_0B_{\log}}-48C^2\\
&\ge-C_0-48C^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{28}
$$
The final inequality is \((\sqrt{B_{\log}}-\sqrt{C_0})^2\ge0\). The argument includes zero bounded-score factors, no labels, and no retained bins.

It remains to carry (28) through the actual original-product halfspaces. We verify this directly for the chosen rows, rather than apply a full-row theorem to a selection. Every \(R_{i,j}^*\) is symmetric about \(j\) and contains \(j\). Its geometric row law is a probability law preserved by reflection; reflection reverses the score. Thus \(\mathbb E_{\kappa_{i,j}^*}Y_{i,j}=0\), including singleton rows. Direct substitution gives the exact likelihood identities
$$
\log\frac{\kappa_{i,j}^*(x)}{p_{i,x}}
=-\log H_i^*(j)-Y_{i,j}(x),\qquad
p_{i,x}=H_i^*(j)\kappa_{i,j}^*(x)e^{Y_{i,j}(x)}.
\tag{29}
$$
Consequently the expected log likelihood ratio under \(\kappa_{i,j}^*\) is \(-\log H_i^*(j)\) and its variance is \(V_{i,j}^*\). These are the selected-row versions of the identities in 445a9e668ee1a705. They retain the original probability \(p_{i,x}=w_{i,x}/Z_i\). In particular
$$
b_i^*=\frac1{Z_i^3}\sum_{j\in A_i}w_{i,j}
\left(\sum_{x\in R_{i,j}^*}\sqrt{w_{i,x}w_{i,2j-x}}\right)^2,
\tag{30}
$$
with the full original \(Z_i\) and all center atoms.

For a supported product center \(\mathbf j=(j_1,\ldots,j_L)\), put
$$
\begin{aligned}
R_{\mathbf j}^*&=\prod_iR_{i,j_i}^*,&
H_P^*(\mathbf j)&=\prod_iH_i^*(j_i),&
\kappa_{\mathbf j}^*&=\bigotimes_i\kappa_{i,j_i}^*,\\
Y_{\mathbf j}(X)&=\sum_iY_{i,j_i}(x_i),&
\sigma_{\mathbf j}^2&=\sum_iV_{i,j_i}^*.
\end{aligned}
\tag{31}
$$
Independence and the zero score means give
\(\mathbb E_{\kappa_{\mathbf j}^*}Y_{\mathbf j}=0\) and
\(\mathbb E_{\kappa_{\mathbf j}^*}Y_{\mathbf j}^2=\sigma_{\mathbf j}^2\). Multiplying (29) gives, for every \(X\in R_{\mathbf j}^*\),
$$
P_X=H_P^*(\mathbf j)\kappa_{\mathbf j}^*(X)e^{Y_{\mathbf j}(X)}
=\frac{\prod_iw_{i,x_i}}{\prod_iZ_i}.
\tag{32}
$$
The auxiliary law in (31) has not replaced the original product in this equality.

Every closed ambient halfspace containing \(\mathbf j\) contains at least one endpoint of each distinct reflected pair \(X,2\mathbf j-X\). Otherwise its defining linear inequality would strictly exclude both endpoints and hence their midpoint. It also contains \(\mathbf j\). The simultaneous reflection preserves the selected product row and its geometric law, and negates \(Y_{\mathbf j}\). Summing the smaller original mass in each noncentral orbit and half the central mass therefore proves
$$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_P(\mathbf j)
&\ge\frac12\sum_{X\in R_{\mathbf j}^*}
\min\lbrace P_X,P_{2\mathbf j-X}\rbrace\\
&=\frac{H_P^*(\mathbf j)}2
\mathbb E_{\kappa_{\mathbf j}^*}e^{-|Y_{\mathbf j}|}
\ge\frac{H_P^*(\mathbf j)}2e^{-\sigma_{\mathbf j}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{33}
$$
The last inequality is Jensen followed by Cauchy--Schwarz. The oriented sum counts each noncentral pair twice before its factor \(1/2\), and the central atom once before that factor. Thus (33) includes every boundary halfspace and uses no positive-variance or full-dimensionality assumption.

Let \(q^*=\bigotimes_iq_i^*\). All these center laws are defined because their rows contain their positive-mass central atoms. The exact identities
\(P_{\mathbf j}H_P^*(\mathbf j)^2=(\prod_i b_i^*)\prod_iq_{i,j_i}^*\) and
\(\mathbb E_{q^*}\sigma_{\mathbf j}^2=\sum_i\nu_i^*\)
give, by squaring (33), summing under the original \(P\), and using Jensen and Cauchy--Schwarz once more,
$$
\begin{aligned}
M_2(P)
&\ge\frac14\left(\prod_i b_i^*\right)
\mathbb E_{q^*}e^{-2\sigma_{\mathbf j}}\\
&\ge\frac14\left(\prod_i b_i^*\right)
\exp\left(-2\sqrt{\sum_i\nu_i^*}\right)\\
&=\frac14\left(\prod_i k_i^{-2}\right)
\exp\left(S_g-2\sqrt{\sum_i\nu_i^*}\right)
\ge c\prod_i k_i^{-2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{34}
$$
The last step is (28) and the definition (1). Jensen under the same original law now gives
\(M_3(P)=\mathbb E_P(\tau_P^2)^{3/2}\ge M_2(P)^{3/2}\ge c^{3/2}\prod_i k_i^{-3}\).
For the common-pair assertion every \(k_i=K_i\), proving (5). For the four-weight assertion \(k_i\le2^{n_i}\), proving (9). In particular neither a factorwise moment coefficient nor separate coefficients for the three groups were multiplied.

Finally consider the stated four-height application, keeping \(\mathcal A_s=\lbrace x\in A:H(x)=s\rbrace\) as in 2fb7953b22f4b674. Its classification of unequal-height same-parity pairs can be checked directly without atomic activity. Completeness forces each same-parity midpoint into \(A\). The six possible averages of unequal heights from \(\lbrace0,a,b,2b\rbrace\) are
\(a/2,b/2,b,(a+b)/2,b+a/2,3b/2\).
Under \(0<a<b/4\), only \(b\), the average of \(0\) and \(2b\), is occupied: \(a/2\in(0,a)\), \(b/2,(a+b)/2\in(a,b)\), and \(b+a/2,3b/2\in(b,2b)\). Thus every unequal-weight same-parity pair has raw endpoint weights \(e^{-2tb}\) and \(1\), and exact midpoint products follow from the affine log weight. These factors satisfy the common-pair hypothesis with \(T=tb\), so even the occupied-capacity bound (5) applies. Their ambient capacity is still \(2^n\), exactly as in 2fb7953b22f4b674; it has not been identified with their possibly smaller occupied count. This establishes the requested four-height consequence and completes the theorem.
statement:
Set \(T_0=\log4096=2\log64\) and \(C=256\). Write \(C_{\mathrm{occ}}(M,T)\) for the finite constant called \(C(M,T)\) in accepted fact 31c9b0b9219d18d9, and put
$$
C_0=C_{\mathrm{occ}}(2,T_0),\qquad
c=\frac14\exp(-48C^2-C_0)>0.
\tag{1}
$$
These are absolute constants.

First let \(L\ge1\) and \(n_1,\ldots,n_L\ge1\) be integers. For every \(i\), let \(A_i\subseteq\mathbb Z^{n_i}\) be finite and nonempty, with positive raw weights \(w_{i,x}\) on its entire support. Assume each ambient parity class contains at most two atoms. Whenever distinct \(x,y\in A_i\) have the same coordinatewise parity, require
$$
j=\frac{x+y}{2}\in A_i,\qquad w_{i,j}^{\,2}=w_{i,x}w_{i,y}.
\tag{2}
$$
For every factor having an unequal-weight same-parity pair, suppose there are fixed numbers \(0<u_i<v_i\) such that every such pair has endpoint-weight multiset \(\lbrace u_i,v_i\rbrace\). Factors with no unequal-weight same-parity pairs are allowed. There is no restriction on the other weight values, the number of exact weight levels, or the number of pairs with a common midpoint.

Retain the original normalizers, laws, and occupied parity counts
$$
\begin{aligned}
Z_i&=\sum_{x\in A_i}w_{i,x},& p_{i,x}&=\frac{w_{i,x}}{Z_i},&
K_i&=\bigl|\lbrace x+2\mathbb Z^{n_i}:x\in A_i\rbrace\bigr|,\\
P&=\bigotimes_{i=1}^L p_i,& N&=\sum_{i=1}^L n_i,&
P_{(x_1,\ldots,x_L)}&=\frac{\prod_iw_{i,x_i}}{\prod_iZ_i}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$
All laws are extended by zero off their supports. With the actual ambient-halfspace conventions of accepted fact 445a9e668ee1a705, define
$$
\tau_P(\mathbf j)=\inf\lbrace P(\mathcal H):
\mathcal H\subseteq\mathbb R^N\text{ is a closed halfspace containing }\mathbf j\rbrace,
\qquad M_r(P)=\sum_{\mathbf j}P_{\mathbf j}\tau_P(\mathbf j)^r.
\tag{4}
$$
Then
$$
M_2(P)\ge c\prod_iK_i^{-2},\qquad
M_3(P)\ge c^{3/2}\prod_iK_i^{-3}.
\tag{5}
$$

Here is the common-score estimate underlying (5). Suppress the factor index, so \(K\) is its occupied parity count. Retain the full reflected quantities of 445a9e668ee1a705, and define their same-weight selections by
$$
\begin{aligned}
R_j&=\lbrace x\in A:2j-x\in A\rbrace,&
H_p(j)&=\sum_{x\in R_j}\sqrt{p_xp_{2j-x}},&
b(p)&=\sum_{j\in A}p_jH_p(j)^2,\\
\kappa_j(x)&=\frac{\sqrt{p_xp_{2j-x}}}{H_p(j)},&
Y_j(x)&=\frac12\log\frac{p_x}{p_{2j-x}},&
V_j&=\mathbb E_{\kappa_j}Y_j^2,\\
q_j&=\frac{p_jH_p(j)^2}{b(p)},&
\nu&=\sum_{j\in A}q_jV_j,\\

One always has \(E\ge1/4\) and \(F\ge1\). If \(E<1\), there is an unequal-weight pair, so its common weights \(u,v\) are defined. Put

Second, the same constant \(c\) has the following broader ambient-capacity consequence. For every \(i\), suppose \(A_i=Q_i\cap\mathbb Z^{n_i}\) is finite and nonempty for a convex \(Q_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\), each parity class has at most two atoms, and

Without any affine-dimension, gap, atomic-activity, or midpoint-multiplicity restriction, the original product in (3) satisfies
$$
M_2(P)\ge c4^{-N},\qquad M_3(P)\ge c^{3/2}8^{-N}.
\tag{9}

The occupied-capacity conclusion (5) is asserted under the common mixed-pair hypothesis; (9) is the ambient conclusion for the broader four-weight class.

In particular, (5) and (9) apply to the four-height class of 2fb7953b22f4b674 without its assumption \(2^{2n_i}\sum_xp_{i,x}^3<1\): each \(A_i=Q_i\cap\mathbb Z^{n_i}\) is finite, nonempty, and of affine dimension \(n_i\), with at most two atoms per parity class; \(H_i:\mathbb Z^{n_i}\to\mathbb Z\) is primitive with occupied heights exactly \(\lbrace0,a_i,b_i,2b_i\rbrace\); \(a_i,b_i\) are positive coprime integers with \(0<a_i<b_i/4\); and \(w_{i,x}=e^{-t_iH_i(x)}\), where \(t_i>0\), \(t_ib_i\ge\log64\), and \(t_ia_i<\log64\).
